speechtext: Hon. WILLIAM PUGSLEY (Minister of Public Works) moved that the second and final report of the joint restaurant committee be adopted.
What are the functions of the committee?

They are set put in the report which was made by the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons, and which was appointed last session. The motion is that their report be adopted, and that these four gentlemen be appointed members of the joint committee. Their duties will be to take charge of the operations of the restaurant, and will be those of the ordinary club committee.
The House would like to have a little information as to these operations. What is it that is going to be established and how is it going to be paid for?
I shall have to get the report of the committee.
Has the report been printed ?

I think not. It was submitted by Mr. Sutherland, and he asked me to make this motion. I regret that Mr. Sutherland is not here as he presented the report, and was on the joint committee of last year when he was Speaker of the House.

There is no very urgent haste in the matter. Perhaps the hon. gentleman will take some means of having that report made available to members in printed or some other form. I appreciate very much what has been done in connection with the placing of the restaurant on a better basis, but at the same time it would be well to know what we are doing before taking these steps.
Has the report been printed in the Votes and Proceedings ?

Yes, a few days ago.
Motion withdrawn.

When will the balance of the evidence taken before Mr. Justice Cassels be printed. There is a very considerable amount of evidence yet to be printed, and it would expedite business if it were placed before the House at an early date so that we might come to a conclusion whether a debate is necessary.

I have asked for a definite statement to-night as to the time it will take to complete them and will try and have definite information for to-morrow.

On the order for House again in committee on the following proposed resolution :
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide that the Governor in Council, upon the recommendation of the head of a department based upon a report of the deputy head, may grant to any officer, clerk or employee under the deputy heads in the inside service as defined by the Civil Service Amendment Act, 1908, who was in the public service at the time of the coming into force of that Act, an increase of salary of $150 a year, subject to the provisions hereinafter contained: that in the case of any officer,

clerk or employee who has received an increase of salary upon organization and classification under the said Act, such increase shall be offset against the increase which such person might otherwise receive under any Act to ibe founded on this resolution; that no increase under any Act to be founded on this resolution to any officer, clerk or employee shall exceed the difference between his present salary and the maximum salary of the subdivision in which he has been placed upon organization and classification under the said Act of 1908; that all increases provided for hereunder shall take effect from the first day of September, 1908; that all sums of money voted by the parliament for the financial year ending on March 31, 1909, and applicable to the payment of salaries or increase of salaries of persons in the inside service shall be applicable to the payment of increases of salary granted under the Act to be founded in this resolution, so far as such sums are not required for the specific purposes for which they were granted; and during the said financial year there may be paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada such moneys required for the payment of increases of salary hereunder as have not been voted by parliament.
^T- FOSTER. Before the Speaker leaves the Chair, I would like to ask the minis-*?r question. I have in my hands a classification of people in the inside service, by Order in Council, 25th of January, 1909, as on the 1st of September, 1908. I find a long list of names with the divisions, and evidently the positions of the different persons, with former salary and proposed salary. Is that all that is contained m the order in council respecting a reclassification of the departments?

So far as I know, it is. I have not looked at this, but I think it is an exact transcription of the order in council. Possibly with slight exceptions, that is all. There may be others. In one case, the Justice Department says, a certain gentleman who had been in" the outside service in receipt of $3,000 a year, must go into subdivision A of the first division, that seems to be absolute under the law. That is an office which, when it ceases to be occupied by the present incumbent, I think ought to be in subdivision B ofi the first division, and I directed that an addendum should be made to the order in council declaring that. There may be others, I do not know.
House went into committee on the resolution.

I find a great deal of difficulty in proceeding with this resolution at the present time, on account of lack of information, and I will frankly explain to my hon. friend where I find the difficulty. This makes provision for adding $150 to each member of the Civil Service who, since the 1st of September, has been upon the establishment books, as I understand Mr. PUGSLEY.
it, and who has not, having been at the head of the class, received already an increase by virtue of classification-that is in brief. Well, of course I dissent from the principle of making a fiat increase without any discrimination as to merit or services. But let that go for the moment. There are other difficulties. For instance, suppose that a gentleman or lady has been appointed to the service on, we will say, the 29th of August; is that person to get the $150 flat increase as well ? That is one question w'hich may do for a time. Again, suppose that on or about that time, or not long before, some person in the department received an increase of $100, $200, $300, $400, $500, and then on the next day, the 1st of September, went into the new classification in his proper place; does that person also get the $150 increase? That stands for another type. Suppose another instance. Suppose that some one who was on the contingency list in one of the departments of the inside service at a very small salary, has desired to get into the classified service at a larger salary, and thereupon resigned his position in the inside service and was appointed a few days before the 1st of September to a position in the inside service at an increased salary, and was then transferred from the outside into the inside service after the 1st day of September; does that person also get an increase ? Also, how many of these different categories are there? Unless we get a straight statement from the minister that none of these three classes, or at least neither of the two classes I mentioned last, are to receive $150 increase under this resolution, I do not know that we are in a position to go on with this Bill. We may be doing a great injustice to certain ersons. That information I have asked for y way of question, and by way of a resolution which has already passed the House. It is impossible in a few days to bring this down; but none of these returns with this information ought to take more than two or three days to be put into shape so that we can have it before the House. I do not like to decide a question like this, with so much involved, on the basis of so little information. I am not trying to block the resolution or the legislation, but it will take a little time any way.

In reply to the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), I recognize the importance of the information for which he has asked, and I think it is quite right that the hon. member and the House should have that information. It will take a few days to get it, perhaps a week, I do not know until I get at it. But I may say now in general terms that the resolution provides for dealing with the service as on the 1st of September. Whether the individual may have been in the position which he occupied on the 1st of

September, one week, or one year, or ten years, there is no provision in this Bill and no intention to go back of the 1st of September. I may say to my hon. friend that I do not wish to enter into the merits of the various questions he has brought up until the information he has asked for is before the House. But I will just say in general terms that after considerable discussion and investigation it was decided to make this Bill a complement of the Bill of last year. That Bill made a change in the Civil Service to take place on the 1st of September; we believe therefore that this Bill should deal with the Civil Service as on the 1st of September. I dare say that there may be a few instances, I could not tell how many, where people may have come into the service, we will say, within a month of the 1st of September; there may be others where they came in within three months, others within a longer time. We did not consider that any other date than the 1st of September would be as proper, or on the whole as just, a date to take. And if we undertook to deal with it at all, we had to fix a date, arbitrarily-if my hon. friend chooses to use that term- for the Act to begin to apply. I think I have answered almost all the suggestions that the hon. gentleman has made of contingencies that might arise. I do not mean to say that this Act is going to give absolutely the same treatment to everybody in the service. I think that every Act that is framed must necessarily have some slight inequalities in its incidence upon individual members of the service. We have discussed the various ways of doing it, and have concluded that this is, perhaps, the manner in which the least inequality wUl arise, and one which is just and fair. If my hon. friend desires it, I can only ask that the committee wait before concluding this matter. But I would suggest to my hon. friend, and other hon. members, that if there are other points on which they would like to have information, they might make them known now, so that I could be prepared to give all the information desired when the matter is taken up for discussion again.

That is perfectly right. So far as I am concerned, I have gone over the matter carefully, and have put the points on which I wished information, and other members can do the same. There is one other point that I would call to the attention of the minister. He proposes to take general power to withdraw from the consolidated revenue fund whatever is required for the payment of these salaries without taking any special vote. I would deprecate that. Last year, when the House passed the Civil Service Bill and passed the estimates also, the session was about to close. It was absolutely impossible, at that time, to tell how much money would be required for the purposes of this Act. Therefore, we gave
general power to the government to take from the consolidated revenue fund whatever might be necessary for the purposes of the Act. But you are in a different position now. The session is only beginning, and you are not face to face with an unknown computation, but can find out exactly what you will need. Therefore, instead of trying to avail itself of this general power, which should only be given in an emergency, the government should bring down an estimate of what is necessary to pay the Bill and have that estimate passed by the House. The minister, I am sure, quite understands that he had better have as few of these anomalies and exceptions as possible, especially in relation to the appropriation of money.

Would the minister be good enough to bring down a statement showing the number of employees brought in from the outside service and placed on the staff under this Act? My reason for asking is to be found in the figures of the estimates. In 1908, the Civil Government estimates amounted to something over $2,060,000. This year the amount is over $3,960,000. In addition, there will be this $347,000 granted to the civil servants under this proposal for a flat increase of $150 each. It is very confusing when you look over the different departments, and have no means of knowing the number of men brought in under this arrangement.
I should be glad to bring that information down.
Would the minister object to having the names given as well?
No objection.

Has the government come to any conclusion or worked out any plan to put all the service on an equal footing? At present it is most unsatisfactory. One department lets its clerks out at four o'clock, and in the adjoining office the clerks work until five o'clock. This has been a source of annoyance in the service for many years past. We are now granting an annual increase to the civil servants amounting to nearly half a million dollars. I do not object to that; I wish to see the civil servants well paid. But when we are doing this, I think it is up to this House to see that the country gets something in return for this large increase. That can be brought about without doing any injustice to any of the civil servants. I claim that the civil servants who go to work at 9.30 a.m.,-and in some of the departments they go at ten o'clock, for I meet them as^ I am coming up town-and leave at four o'clock, with an hour and a half in the middle of the day, are not giving an honest day s work, and are not giving value for the money we are paying them. I think the service should be put on an equal footing. And, in view of the increased salary we are giving,

if the government insisted that the civil servants should be in their offices at nine o'clock, and work until five in the afternoon, with an hour and a half off in the middle of the day, that would not be asking too much. And I want to tell the House that the best officers in the different departments are doing that to-day. The best officers are at work at nine o'clock in the morning, and stay there until five, and many of them until half past five or six o'clock, and even come back in the evening if necessary. Those who do the least while there are those who come the latest and leave the earliest. This is a matter that others _ beside the civil servants are interested in. The whole country is interested, for the country pays the salaries. I would like to have some answer from the minister as to what the government propose to do in that connection.
I am most agreeably surprised at the speech of the hon. member (Mr. Turriff). Yesterday, he had quite a different speech

Not at ail.
Mr. ,T. D. REID. Yes, the hon. gentleman then was quite satisfied that the civil servants should go to work at ten o'clock.
No.
The speech that the hon. gentleman made
Read it.

It was in opposition to the speech that I made. But if he had taken my speech of yesterday, and read it here, he would have seen almost word for word what he has said now. Evidently, he has changed his mind
Not at all.
Certainly. Yesterday he was proving that some of the civil servants stayed as long as half past four, and that was an awful hardship
No, no.
Certainly, he

speechtext: I would call the attention of the hon. gentleman (Mr. J. D. Reid) to the fact that he is referring to a past debate, which is out of order.
I accept your correction, Mr. Chairman. So far as that is epneerned, in the remarks I made yesterday

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Order.
Can't I refer to my own speech ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is a past debate.	,

Then, I withdraw-that also. For my part, I do not wish to find any fault with the civil servants, for I believe they are good men ; but I agree with what the hon. member for Assinibioa (Mr Turriff) has said that to have the Civil Service go to work at 9.30 in the morning-and many of them seem to go at any time between 9.30 and ten-and work until four, with an intermission of an hour and a half in the middle of the day, is not enough. That is only five hours of actual work, and I claim that eight hours would not be an unreasonable time for these men to work. If they went on at nine and quit at five, as I believe they should, it would only be seven hours work, giving them one hour for lunch, as they have in banks and other institutions. In fact, I believe that in banks and other business houses some of the clerks do not even have as long a time as that for lunch. These men not having heavy work or brain work of a sufficiently arduous character to require shorter hours, should put in a reasonable number of hours' work and I agree with what the hon. gentleman has just said that there should be a Bill or some understanding whereby government employees should work a uniform number of hours. If the government do not bring it in I hope some other hon. gentleman will and if he does I shall support it.

The practice is a little different in different departments. I am not prepared to say off hand what it is, but I think the Civil Service Act contains a clause dealing with the hours of work. If not there is a rule laid down under the Act. But I know that the practice is slightly different in different departments. I appreciate the difficulties which arise from that. In my own department some of the officers stayed a little longer than others, it created a great deal of ill-feeling and jealousy and I was obliged to ask my deputy minister to arrange that they should all come in and leave at the same hour. I think there are very few civil servants who do not reach their offices at 9.30, the usual hour at which they are required to be there. There is a book kept in which they have to enter their names with the minute at which they arrive, and the officers who are in charge of the different branches would certainly take to task any civil servant who was frequently arriving after the hour at which he was required to be there. I believe there are rare exceptions-not as many as my hon. friend would indicate. The hours are usually from 9.30 until 4 o'clock, with an hour or an hour and a quarter for lunch. I think in some departments an hour is allowed, and in others an hour and a quarter. I do not know of any department in which an hour and a half is allowed, but I am speaking subject to correction.
That makes a six hour day.

Practically a six hour day, and I think that is the general rule. The question of adding to that, in consequence of the increase in salary now, is one that is worthy of consideration, but it has not been embodied in this resolution, and I doubt,the advisability of it. If it were adopted it ought _ to be by way of an amendment to the Civil Service Act. This resolution is not an amendment to the Civil Service Act. This resolution provides for the introduction of a Bill for one particular thing, and when that one particular thing has been carried out this ceases practically to operate. I did not think it was wise that it should be an amendment to the Civil Service Act because it is of a temporary character and the Civil Service Act is a law which deals with and regulates the Civil Service permanently.
Does it fix the hours?

I do not know whether the Act actually fixes the hours or not. I am not sure; I would have to look it up to see. If it does not, I do not quite know how it is that the hours are fixed. They can be fixed, I suppose, by ministerial orders in the different departments themselves. It would be very much better that they should be uniform, and that they should be fixed in such a way that they would be definite.

It does seem to me that hon. gentlemen in this House must come to the conclusion that the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher) is wrong in his understanding as to the hours of work of the members of the Civil Service. In visiting the different branches of the service we find it difficult to do business because of the non-arrival of members of the Civil Service, and I do think that they should be in their places during the time the House is sitting. We do know that hon. gentlemen are worked very much harder than the civil servants. We also know that their time is very much engaged and that unless they have an opportunity of doing their business in connection with the different departments before ten or half past ten, their business is interfered with. Committees meet at ten o'clock and we have no other time in which to visit the departments. It is the exception to find these men in their places at half past nine. I would suggest that the rule should be that they should be in their places during the time that the House is sitting and that they should arrive at their offices at nine o'clock.
I do not believe it possible that there is a a tab kept upon them. It seems that many of the junior officials come and go just as they choose. I am informed that while
there is a rule regarding the hours of attendance in some cases, in many instances there is no rule and that many officials have almost a free hand. I do not think that any business man could do business as it is done in our departments. As far as the' deputies and heads of the departments are concerned they are conscientious men and do their work properly, but I think that many of the subordinates are not fulfilling the duties of their positions as they would be compelled to do in a bank, or in the commercial world. I think that the servants of the people should attend to their duties just as regularly and as punctually as men are required to do in any other walk ot life. I do not think that civil servants are underpaid. I think that the outside service have much more work to do and much greater responsibility than the inside service. The whole system should be carefully looked into and a better system devised.

I would like to ask the minister a question that I have asked ot several of the older members of this House and to which I have been unable to get a satisfactory answer. I would like to know who comprise the inside service and who the outside service?
I would not like to answer off hand. If my hon friend will read the section of the Act covering that point I think he will see. I could not, off hand, do anything but read the definition in the Act.
I would like to ask the minister if there are any civil servants in Ottawa who were not brought in under the Civil Service Act of last year?

There are in the city of Ottawa the departmental services and also some services which pertain to Ottawa just as similar services pertain to Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg or any other city. The employees of the Ottawa Customs house and the local office of the Inland Revenue Department, for instance, were not brought into the inside service by last year's Bill, but are still in the same position as similar officials in Montreal or Toronto. It is only the departmental services that were brought into the inside service under the Bill of last session. A large number of people were paid out of lump votes of one kind and another in the city of Ottawa in the service and these were all brought in.
Would the minister be good enough to bring in a statement of the number of those in Ottawa who were brought from the outside service into the inside service ?
Certainly.

I would urge the minister to add to the list of those who will receive this increase the railway mail clerks

throughout Canada. They are men _ who loyally perform their duty and who live a hazardous life; they belong to that department which has a surplus, and I do not think there are any harder worked men in [DOT] the Civil Service of Canada than the railway mail clerks.

Before the committee rises, I would ask whether or not the return just handed to us embodies all the conditions of the various orders in council establishing the reorganization of the different departments ?

As far as I know it does; I have not seen the return myself. The instructions were that the orders in council for the reorganization of the departments should all be included. I understand that the Interior Department order is not there as it was not completed. There will have to be also two resolutions of the Senate and of the House of Commons.

I understand that. The statute of last year, section 8, subsection 2, made the following provision:
The order in council shall give the names of the several branches of the department, with the number and character of the offices, clerkships and other positions in each, and the duties, titles and salaries thereafter to pertain thereto.
The return brought down has four headings, first, a name, second the title, character and duties of office or position, third former salary, fourth proposed salary. Under the heading or ' title, character and duties or post or position ' the only thing that I observe is the title of the position which the officer is to fill, and I do not observe anything defining otherwise the character or the duties of the office or position. It seemed to me when we were discussing the matter last year that it would be exceedingly important that the duties of the office should be defined as far as possible. I am not at all insisting that the duties of each officer should be brought down and laid as a return on the table of the House, but I think they ought to be defined in the department, and it seems to me that any order in council dealing with the reorganization of a department which is confined to conferring a title, such as clerk or stenographer or something upon a particular officer and stating whether his salary is the same or greater, is not a compliance with the statute of last year nor does it fulfil one of the principal objects of that statute. I am not so much concerned with the hours of service of the civil servants in Ottawa; in fact I know some institutions where it is absolutely forbidden clerks and employees to do any work after office hours or in the evening for the reason that reasonable hours are given for doing a reasonable amount of work in office hours, and any clerk who is not able to do Mr. LEWIS.
that reasonable amount of work within these reasonable hours is prima facie considered unfit to continue in the service of the institution. I think reasonable hours of service should be assigned, and should be set out with some particularity in order that every person in the service in Canada may know that by virtue of his position in the Civil Service, certain duties are incumbent on him and he must perform this amount of work in office hours, in ordinary conditions at least. I realize that in time of emergency, for instance, during the session, it may be necessary for clerks to work outside of office hours, possibly in the evenings; but the duties should be defined and every clerk should understand that he has certain things to do within certain hours. I mentioned last evening some matters that had been brought to my attention by men previously in the service who stated to me, as one of the crying needs of the service, some means of inspection. I do not know that these orders provide for inspection, but I think the time of the Civil Service Commission might be employed to some extent in that way either through themselves or others. I know that in most great corporations there is a thorough system of inspection by which the heads of the corporation are able to know from time to time, by the reports of competent people, whether every officer of the corporation is able to perform his duties. I was told by a young man not now in the service that the man next to him when he was in one branch of that particular department, occupied nearly all his time in reading novels during the day without any one to inspect or supervise him; and the man next him was occupied in some other manner of as little advantage to the people of this country who were paying him his salary. The same young man told me of another man in the same department who had worked, industriously and indefatigably who had worked after hours night after night and year after year to qualify himself for the duties of his position, who had passed an examination in a certain outside institution which gave him a very high status, and who was working on in the department on a very small salary, having received absolutely no consideration or recognition for the honest, able and indefatigable endeavours which he had made to qualify himself better to serve the people of this country. It is with matters of that kind that if seems to me efforts at reorganization of the departments should be concerned, and I hope that the endeavour of last session to improve the Civil Service of this country will not stop short of some thorough system of inspection such as that employed by some of the great corporations of this country. I trust that my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture will take this into consideration, because I think it is vital and es-

sential to placing the Civil Service on the best possible basis.

I may say to my hon. friend that the Act of last session provided, under certain circumstances, for an inspection ai\d report upon any department by the Civil Service Commissioners. There is not and never has been any provision for regular continuous inspection. I am not prepared to say that that would not be a good thing ; at the same time, I doubt very much the value of it. Such instances as my hon. friend has just adduced are clear evidence that some officials above those described was derelict in his duty. It was the duty of the deputy minister or the chief of the branch in which these persons were employed not to have allowed that kind of thing to go on. I think the responsibilities and duties of the higher officers of the Civil Service would be rather interfered with if any ordinary inspection system were to be adopted; they would perhaps be less inclined to look closely after the details of their administration. I have had opportunities occasionally of administering one or two departments other than my own, and while I have no doubt that while such cases as those mentioned by my hon. friend do occur sometimes, they are rare exceptions to the general rule. As a general rule, the officers of the different departments are kept up to their work by their immediate chiefs, who again are looked after by the deputy minister in a pretty business-like way, though in a large service like this, with upwards of 2,500 employees in Ottawa, a few instances of the kind mentioned may occur, instances which is is hard to overcome. There may be some body who is intolerably lazy or inefficient, and if he were to be dismissed from the service at a time when he could not go on the superannuation list, and after he had been paying into the superannuation fund for a good many years, with perhaps a family dependent upon him, such an action might seem unduly severe. It requires a good deal of determination and perhaps hard heartedness to visit such a man with the just measure which his delinquencies would properly bring down upon his head. But I believe the instances of that kind in the service are rare, and, as a general rule, while the hours are shorter than those in commercial life, and while the salaries are pretty good in comparison, the average civil servant gives a fair return for the salary he is paid; the service is efficient, and the business of the country well carried on. I had an opportunity during the last year of studying closely, in writings at any rate, the systems of the United States and Great Britain, and I venture to say that today the public service of Canada is carried on more economically and more efficiently, in proportion to the number of men employed than the service of either of those two countries.

I cannot concur in the view which my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture has advanced as to the possible results of a system of inspection. Under a system such as is carried out in a bank, when a branch is examined, and it is found that any of the subordinate officials are not performing their duties in a satisfactory way, that fact is set down as a black mark against the chief of that branch whose duty it wras to see that the subordinates properly performed their duties. Therefore, a system of inspection, instead of lessening the supervision of the man in charge of the subordinates, ought to increase it.

As I understand, under the Act the theoretical organization of the departments is left to the deputies themselves; the duties appertaining to each office and the salary attached to it are prescribed. In trying to improve the service, why not adopt the system of inspection that exists in England? Why not also adopt the system of registration that exists there? This will show what every man in every department does every day, and the commission could ascertain whether he has being doing his duty or not. You may have efficient heads of the departments, but unless you have a registration of the duties and the work done by each officer you will always have pets in the department who will do nothing while the others will be doing the work.

I may say that the Act of last session provided for a record of the clerks to be kept. There was nothing of that kind in the former Civil Service Act. The Act of last session did not go perhaps as far as my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Haggart) suggests, and I do not for a moment say that what he suggests is going too far; but it did provide for a record of the work of every clerk, so that when his name came up for promotion or increase of salary, that record could be referred to.

I notice running through the papers the last few days some very strange statements with regard to the system of overcharging civil servants for loans. The statement is made by members of the service and parties outside that the departments are the happy hunting ground of loan sharks, especially on pay days. If that be the case, some deputy head or other officer is very lax. The government buildings should not be allowed to be used for business of that description. No doubt when a civil servant is approached by gentlemen of this kind before his fellow colleagues, such insistent gentlemen can get what they like, especially if the official be a little sensitive. Somebody ought to take this mat-

ter in hand and see that traps are set in these preserves for that kind of poacher.

I quite agree with my hon. friend. Some years ago it came to my knowledge that a certain individual was pursuing some of the clerks in my department and I gave instructions that he was not to be allowed to come in at all. I do not think that the departmental offices are the places for that kind of business. It is private business which ought to be done elsewhere and outside office hours. I have read the accounts in the paper and agree that the thing should be put a stop to; but how to stop it I am not prepared to say. No doubt many of those who are in the clutches of the usurers, if they are usurers, have got there by reason of their extreme weakness or more or less laxness in their conduct.
They are often unfortunate.

No doubt, but very often their indebtedness is due to gambling and other things they ought not to indulge in. The matter comes within the administration of the criminal law in this province. As I am not a lawyer, I cannot well give an opinion as to how it should be dealt with. But in the public interest the thing ought to be stopped because no man who is in "the clutches of an usurer, and is deeply in debt, can do good work for his employer. In this ease it is the country which is the employer, and the heads of the departments should do what they can to prevent that kind of work going on inside of their departments.

The record is not such a one as my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Haggart) has mentioned. It is simply a record of the efficiency and conduct of the employees. It does not show what work they are doing.

Their efficiency would be gauged by the amount of work they do. If one clerk' did only half as much of the same kind of routine work as another, he would be called inefficient and the other efficient.

It seems to me that a report every three months by the chiefs of the branches to the deputy head on the efficiency and conduct of the employees does not give much information as to the work they do. It does not give any record of what mechanical work they perform.

I hope the hon. minister will not lose sight of what I mentioned, namely, that the orders in council do not seem to prescribe the duties in accordance with what the statute demands.

PATERSON (Minister of Cus toms) moved that the House go into Committee of Supply.

I intend to take up the time of the House for a few minutes in calling attention to a very important matter. Had I thought the House would have gone into Committee of Supply to-day, I would have notified the government of the item I proposed to bring to the attention of the House, and I regret I have not been able to do so. But the subject is one of so much importance to my mind that I hope we shall have further opportunity of discussing it in this House. I read in the last annual report of the Canadian Pacific Railway the following clause:
To be in a position to provide additional money from this source (issue of stock), if and when necessary, your directors thought it wise to ask the consent of the Governor General in Council to a further increase of ordinary capital stock from $150,000,000 to $200,000,000. This consent has been formally given.
In other words, the Canadian Pacific Railway, the greatest institution in this country, has been given authority, according to the statements of its president, to increase its capital stock from $150,000,000 to $200,000,000. Whether that be so or not, I have only the authority of the president of that company; but in the 'Globe' newspaper of the other day I found this statement:
Small holders of the Canadian Pacific write to 'The Globe' asking why the company cannot give some information as to the basis upon which the new common stock will be issued. Possibly the best answer is that the company itself must first ask the Canadian Parliament for authority to issue the stock. The Canadian Pacific might not be able to say that it was the business of no outsider what method it used to raise new capital, and at the same time benefit its proprietors. It might be able to say this if there were no Railway Commission to fix freight rates, having regard to the profits earned and capital actually invested. The Railway Commission must take into consideration the rights enjoyed by shareholders as well as the dividend return, when considering the application of shippers for the reduction of freight carrying charges. Nevertheless it would be well to remember that in spite of its wealth the C.P.R. is face to face with a good deal of competition, and to meet this will require all the money the road can secure. If the directors prefer to give the shareholders what is practically a stock dividend, instead of a money bonus, from the land fund for instance, they might very easily justify their position. While its control is here, the great bulk of C.P.R. stock is held abroad, and is in the hands of very important interests. It would be unfortunate if the company was

forced to take any position which the foreign shareholders would consider as unfair to them, as the confidence of European and British investors alone has maintained the premier Canadian stock at a high level, and has Been the means of bringing the country itself to the favourable attention of foreign financial centres.
I propose to show to the House that it is of the utmost importance to the people of this country how the capitalization of our railways is increased, and that, for that reason, there ought to be some control of the government over the issue of securities by railway companies. I shall show that the Act for that purpose passed in the State of Hew York in 1897 has been of the utmost advantage to the people of the State. Can it be shown that the giving to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company of power to increase its capital stock from $150,000,000 to $200,000,000 without imposing conditions was of advantage to the public ? I contend that it is in the public interest that such new capitalization should be in the form of bonds, and not in the form of stock. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company could borrow on bonds, probably, at 4 per cent, but if it floats stock, it expects to put aside in its net earnings at least 10 per cent to cover the interest on that stock. I propose also to show that, if the company is allowed to issue stock, that stock should be sold to the public at the highest rate it will bring, and all the money realized should be put into the treasury. But the proposition, as I understand it, is that the ancient and discredited example of the American railways should be followed, and that the issue of stock should be of the nature of what is called ' cutting a melon ' for the benefit of the stockholders. In other words, this $50,000,000, which would bring, perhaps, 150 on the market-it is quoted at about 175 and has been as high as 200-shall be issued at par, which will have the effect of dividing $25,000,000 taken from the people of Canada among the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and that this flotation shall be added to the money on which the shareholders ate drawing- 7- per cent with prospects of still greater earnings. I contend, therefore, that, especially when a company is as well established as the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, its issue of securities should be in the form or bonds, but, if stock is to be issued, it should be put upon the market for what it will bring, and the money used for the benefit of the road. I totally agree with this idea of ' cutting a melon ' representing $25,000,000 for the benefit of the shareholders, and especially do I denounce it in connection with a company like the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, which has already been so heavily bonused in money and land, given a great franchise. I learn from the ' Statist ' and the ' Economist/ the two 14
leading financial papers of England, that the Canadian Pacific Railway to-day is establishing surplus earnings equal to 10 per cent on its stock. If it is the intention of the company to take that much out of the traffic earnings, I think that charge is altogether unfair. Suppose that the company wants $50,000,000, as the president says it soon will; if it availed itself of the current price of stock, even discounting to-day's quotation by 25 points, it could raise the money by an issue of $37,500,000 of stock. Or, if it issued $50,000,000 of bonds, it could raise the money at 4 per cent, an annua? charge of $2,000,000. In the form in which they propose to issue it, this will represent a fixed charge upon the earnings of the road, paid by the people, of this country of $5,000,000 a year, or $3,000,000 more than should be paid, and this proposed method of issue capitalized, represents $75,000,000. In other words, this proposal, which some people ignore or say is of no moment, means that the passenger and freight rates of the Canadian Pacific Railway are to be burdened, quite unnecessarily, with a' fixed charge to pay interest on $75,000,000. For, no railway maintains itself except out of the charges it makes upon the public, and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company proposes to take from the public, by this unfair, improvident and improper flotation, enough to pay the interest on $75,000,000. Only 38 per cent of the net income of the Canadian Pacific Railway is required to pay the interest on its bond issue. Why should not 60 or even 70 per cent of the net income be used to pay interest on bonds ? To maintain a proper equilibrium between the stock and bond issues, at least 75 per cent of the net earnings should be devoted to the payment of interest on the bonds. If this issue is allowed, there must be heavy unnecessary traffic charges. It cannot be otherwise. The State of California has made the announcement that because of the improper watering of stock of the railways in that state by Mr. Harriman, the traffic charges have had to *be advanced by the amount of $10,000,000 to pay the interest on that water. I have been told that this is no concern of the people. But I contend that it is every concern of the people, for freight charges are based upon fixed charges, interest and dividend charges, and, unless the greatest care is exercised in authorizing these flotations the public will suffer. To show that the public have suffered, I think I can say v ith perfect fairness that the financial troubles of the last few years in the United States have been largely due to the over-capitalization of corporations, and especially railway corporations. Dividends have to be paid on all this water, and the money has to come out of the people.
To show that the American people are not neglectful of the situation, I wish to



point out that in 1897 the state of New York, perhaps following the good example of Canada, established a railway commission, which to my mind is the finest piece of legislation I know of in New York state. I also wish to say that we have in Canada an excellent Railway Commission, and my object mainly here to-day is to see that the government put into their railway law the legislation which has been put into the law of the State of New York governing these things. I will read the provision in the New York law. Section 55 of the Public Service Commissions Act reads as follows:
A common carrier

For instance the Canadian Pacific Railway corporation. [DOT]

or street railroad corporation organized
or existing, or hereafter incorporated, under or by virtue of the laws of the State of New York, may issue stocks, bonds, notes or other evidence of indebtedness payable at periods of more than twelve months after the date thereof, when necessary for the acquisition of property, the construction, completion, extension or improvement of its facilities, or for the improvement or maintenance of its service or for the discharge or lawful refunding of its obligations, provided and not otherwise that there should have been secured from the proper commission an order authorizing such issue, and the amount thereof and stating that, in the opinion of the commission, the use of the capital to be secured by the issue of such stock, bonds, notes or other evidence of indebtedness is reasonably required for the said purposes of the corporation, for the purpose of enabling it to determine whether it should issue such an order, the commission should make inquiry or investigation, hold such hearings and examine such witnesses, books, papers, documents or contracts as it may deem of importance in enabling it to reach a determination.
Now that I contend should be our law. The Governor in Council, when this $50,000,000 was authorized, if it has been authorized, should have exercised some discretion and probably would, if we had it in our law. My chief object in bringing this matter before the House to-day is to urge upon the government the insertion of a clause in the Railway Commission Act of Canada which will give the Railway Commission authority to control all such issues, and that the railways, before they can get such authority, shall be obliged to establish that it is in the public interest that the authority be given. Though that Act was only passed in the United States in 1897, and the commission was organized less than 18 months ago, they have had before them up to the latest date I could get, seven applications for an increase in stock and issue of bonds. It is a very illuminative thing to read the findings of the commission on these various applications. I will read two or three short paragraphs from them. For instance, on an application of a company on April 7, in Mr. W. F. MACLEAN.
connection with the Lehigh & Hudson River Railway, and on which decision was given May 7 last, there is this statement, and the commission is living up to it.
It is sufficient for present purposes to call attention to the fact that some obligations may be the proper subject of capitalization and other obligations may not be. One purpose of the Public Service Commissioners Law is to restrain and limit the hitherto irrepressible elasticity of corporate capitalization to the matters which may properly be capitalized, and the same discriminating scrutiny should and will be extended to indebtedness as to other subjects enumerated in that statute.
Now the same sin, and it is a great public and political sin, prevails in Canada today; that sin is the hitherto irrepressible elasticity of corporate capitalization, it must be restrained, it must be limited, it must be directed in channels which will make the least charge on the railway, and therefore on the public. It has got so bad in the United States, as I said before, that the financial panic we have heard so much of is said to be due to this extensive and improper capitalization People say that Roosevelt is the man who brought on the panic in the United States. I say that the panic in the United States is largely due to this over-capitalization that has taken place there; and it will disarrange our finances here and it will make our railway charges here exorbitant if we do not check it. I say the time has arrived when we ought to check it in this country. Here is another deliverance of the Railway Commission in New York:
In other words our order should not operate to increase the interest charges upon this property by one per cent or any per cent for the next sixteen years without some corresponding increase in the company's assets in property or in cash to be devoted to the construction and improvement covered by the case under consideration. Indeed it may be questioned whether a present low interest bearing bond should be permitted to be retired by a bond bearing higher interest in any event when the present bond would run a reasonable period before maturity.
The Railway Commission in the United States says that a railroad company should not even be allowed to substitute a bond of a high rate for one of a lower rate, because it knows that every such increase of that kind is to the detriment of the people and must end in the increase of freight rates. New, if we are to work out the great object that we had in view in establishing this Railway Commission-and we are working it out, the commission is doing good service in this country every day, and I give the government credit for enforcing that commission fairly and strengthening it in different directions-but if it is to do what we intended it to do, that is, to regulate the

freight charges of this country, it must also do another thing, and regulate the security issues of the companies if it wishes to keep the freight rates at a reasonable figure. If unnecessary capital is issued, or if stock at a high dividend rate is issued where a low interest bearing bond will do, we are simply failing to effect a cure, we are stopping a leak at one end and allowing a leak at the other. My main object to-day is to bring to the attention of the government this statement which is made in the Canadian Pacific Railway annual report, that the authority has already been given, and also to draw the attention of the government to the need of making a provision in the Canadian Railway Act which will give the Commission full power to pass judgment on all the proposed increases of capital and bonds of any railway company in this country. I have heard it argued in this House that it is no concern of the people what the amount of stock issue may be. I say it is of great concern to the people, not only the amount of the issue but the character of the issue; and when a railway is once established, its issue for development and extension purposes ought largely to be confined to bonds instead of stock. I say it will be a scandal, a scandal that no public man can justify, if there is to be perpetrated in a few days, as I believe there will be, the cutting of this ' melon ' whereby $50,000,000 of securities are to be issued to the shareholders at par. It is not in the public interest, it is not to the credit of parliament that the law should remain as it is to-day. I ask the government to give the most careful consideration to this state of affairs, and that before this session is over, indeed before this thing can be perpetrated, if the authority has been given, in some way it should be regulated, and that no increase of security shall be allowed until the reasons for that increase, and the nature of the security that is to be issued, shall pass the scrutiny and receive the sanction of the Board of Railway Commissioners of this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very much interested in the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. W. F. Maclean) who has again shown that he pays particular attention to the way in which large corporations are managed and particularly to the railway problem. The question of the financing of these very large concerns is one that cannot be settled off hand and cannot be managed unless it be by men who have given it a great deal of attention and who, year after year, have profited by the experienced gained. It will go without saying, no matter what any person may think of certain lines of conduct, of the Canadian Pacific Railway, that it is one of the best managed companies in the known world today. While we want to maintain our rights 144
as a people there is one condition that we must maintain, and that is that the credit of the undertakings of the Canadian people and on behalf of Canadian people must stand high in the markets of the world. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company has carried out its undertakings in a marvellous degree. When it was first launched there were differences of opinion as to how it should be done no doubt, and honest differences of opinion. * They had their difficulties in the beginning, in the carrying out of the construction of the road, and they had their financial questions to grapple with. The parliament of Canada assisted them to an extent that it was thought by the majority, at least, was justified. But, leaving all that aside, up to the present time, the Canadian Pacific management stands out as one of the best in this or any other country. When this company, after years of experience, finds that the interests of the people in one particular portion of the Dominion demand a further extension of railway accommodation, it is their business, it is their duty to the people of Canada to, as far as possible, acquiesce in that request and give the people of the great west the railway accommodation that they are asking for. No person will take any exception to that. The only question that can be raised in connection with it is that we regret that the railway companies are not able to give the accommodation as rapidly as the great needs of the west demand that they should, and it is our duty, not only as a government, but as a parliament, to aid any company as far as we possibly can in the endeavour to bring the markets of the world as close as possible to the doors of the people who have gone into our unsettled country in the western part of Canada. We have spent a large amount of money and we are to-day spending large amounts of money to do that very thing. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company come to the government and ask them to allow them to increase their capital stock. What for?-in order that they may yield to that demand and obtain the capital to build lines into parts of the country that do not now have railway accommodation. The necessity of this, ot course, need not be argued for a moment, because every one agrees that it is necessary. But my hon. friend takes exception, to the way in which it is done. I may say there is room for argument as to which is the better method; there is no doubt in the world about that. But the government on this occasion followed the examples and lines they have always followed with regard to increases in capital stock. If a company come, make a good case, and state that they want to extend their line for the benefit of the people or to take care of the traffic of the country, we have always given them an opportunity to do it in this way. This
42$

is no new departure. This is the old line of conduct. Whether it is the better way or not is open to argument, and I was glad to hear the remarks of my hon. friend with regard to it. The men who are engaged in large undertakings, in the management and securing of capital, particularly in a time like this, must take into account the difference in cost or interest between issuing new stock and selling bonds. But is there not another difference? Is there not a difference between placing a new mortgage on a property that now exists and extending the sphere of the proprietorship? The stockholders are the proprietors; the bondholders are the holders of what we might commonly call a mortgage on property and there is a difference. It might make a marked difference in the value of the stock of the Canadian Pacific Railway and in the credit of the company itself if they were to issue a large amount of bonds at any price in order to raise more funds to extend the lines of the company. We must most certainly, as far as possible, keep intact the credit of the company, and we are part proprietors of the great Canadian Pacific Railway in this country, and the better way to keep their credit intact, the better way to advance it, as far as the effect on the market and the stock is concerned, will be by an issue of stock rather than by another large bond issue. It strikes me that those in the financial world, particularly when the finances of the world are in a sensitive condition, will look at it in that way, and while I admit that it is open for argument, I contend that there is a strong argument from the financial standpoint in favour of an issue of stock rather than another large bond issue. My hon. friend very rightly refers to New York state, but this much must be remembered, that it is a far more difficult thing, ordinarily speaking, to finance an undertaking in a new country where the opportunity for traffic is much less than in a thickly settled country
The Canadian Pacific Railway has the best credit in the world.
Yes, because it is managed along the lines I have indicated rather than along the lines that my hon. friend has indicated.
No, they have issued bonds heretofore, but they have quit doing it.

I know. In Canada we have a very small population per mile of railway. No country has as great a mileage of railway per head of population as the Dominion of Canada, but to reverse it, no country in the world to-day has a greater tract of territory per mile of railway than has the Dominion of Canada.

We are a very large country with a comparatively small population. New York state has a very dense population, and California has likewise. In the states of the union to which my hon. friend referred the density of population gives the railways a traffic which the Canadian Pacific Railway, or any other road in this country, cannot expect to have for years. In other words, the Canadian Pacific Railway, as well as other railways in Canada, are dealing with what is to be in the future rather than what is at the present time, and it is necessary for them to be given every opportunity by the government and parliament of Canada to retain their financial position which stands high in the world to-day. In granting this extra issue of stock, as I said before, the government have done what they have done before, not in the dark, not in secret, but in the open, prepared to bring down the order in council if necessary and prepared to explain why this has been done. I say again, we think it was the wisest thing to do; it is, of course, open for argument, as my hon. friend has said, but under all the circumstances I would be prepared as head of the Railway Department to do the same thing again, to allow the Canadian Pacific Railway under present circumstances to obtain this money in order to extend its lines into the great Northwest country where they need more railway facilities.
My hon. friend (Mr. W. F. Maclean) has raised one other important point, that is the question of referring questions of this kind to the Board of Railway Commissioners. There is a good deal to be said in favour of that course, and I promise my hon. friend that I shall give the suggestion the consideration of which it is worthy. There is, however, this further question whether the government that is responsible to the people-more directly responsible in Canada than are the members of the American government who do not have to go to the people for election, while we are constantly in contact with them-should decide on cases of that kind, or whether, they should be referred to the Railway Commission for first consideration, coming to us for final decision. I promise my friend to give the whole question full consideration.

Mr. Speaker, the question introduced by the hon. member for York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) is one that has been before this House for a great number of years. It was debated again and again in the Railway Committee where Mr. Mulock drew attention to the increased rates to which the people of the country must be subjected by reason of the watering of stock or the increased issue of bonds or stock. The hon. gentleman says that there is legislation in the United States against any issues of this kind. That may

be perfectly right, such matters may be left to the Railway Commission as the Minister of Railways suggests to judge whether it is or is not right that an issue of stock or of preferential securities should be made in a certain way, but the Railway Commission have jurisdiction over all these matters and it is their duty to see that the people who eventually have to pay for these things, pay for only the actual cash which has been invested in the undertaking and do not pay the fancy prices that the railways put on their securities.
What are the facts in reference to the particular thing of which the hon. member complains, an issue of a certain amount of stock, I think $50,000,000 to build 600 or 700 miles of railway in the Northwest ? If that money was to be raised on the undertaking itself it could not be raised on any better terms than it is now being raised. The undertaking of this work lessens the property which the present owners of the Canadian Pacific Railway have-

It lessens it to the value of the undertaking, and have not the owners of the road a right to take that into consideration in awarding the stock to the new proprietors? But if they do as they do in some places' in the United States and may do in Canada, it is the duty of our commission to see that in fixing the rates for these roads the fair consideration shall be the actual amount of cash that has been put into the undertaking. The principal reason for seeking to prevent the watering of stock is the idea that some day or other the country will become possessors of the railways. If the railways were taken over by the state their valuation would not be fixed at all on watered stock but would be fixed as in the case of any other undertaking or corporation on the basis of what it is worth as a going concern at the moment it is taken over. That is the consideration and the only consideration with the government. It may have an effect on some people owing to the fear that the railways will exact higher freight and passenger rates from the people because a price has been given to the stock which does not correspond to the value of the property or, in other words, the security has been watered. But to guard against such a result as that, we have appointed a commission for the purpose of protecting the people of the country in these matters.
In reference to the particular matter at issue, the people of this country desire the building of 600 miles of railway in the Northwest. How are they to get the money? Can they raise it on the undertaking itself?
On the whole property of the concern.

You raise it on the whole property. Then have not I, as a stockholder in the Canadian Pacific Railway, a right to consider whether the building of that property would affect the security that I have ? That is the primary consideration and the holders of Canadian Pacific Railway securities have a right to decide upon it. The only consideration worthy the attention of the people of this country is that in the eventuality of the state becoming the possessor of the railways they shall get them at their proper price and value. This is provided for in nearly every Railway Act of the British parliament. I admit to a certain extent with the hon. member for York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) that the tendency of legislation in this country and of ideals throughout the world is that in all matters of transport the people of the country should have control either by ownership, or as we have done here in this country, by the people ruling the railways through a commission in regard to the fixing of rates.
All these attacks upon property are not a benefit or essential to the people of this country.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.
It is not an advantage to have these matters discussed on the lines pursued by my hon. friend here.
Oh, oh.

The proper line is to take a reasonable view of what is necessary in the interest of the country and I think that it is in the interest of the country even on the proposition laid down by my hon. friend, that this legislation should pass.

There are two things that ought to be taken into consideration when such 3, proposal is made, either to the Governor in Council or to the Railway Commission. It seems to me that the first question is the money needed and for what purpose ? Is it for the purpose of better accommodating the public or providing some want which up to that time has not been provided ? And the second, if this obligation is to be incurred, how can you best raise the money so that the smaller amount wall do as much good as a larger amount raised in some other way. It seems to me that it resolves itself into this. We have given the Canadian Pacific Railway and every other corporation of the kind a large consideration in money and lands to provide services for the public and therefore the country has an interest 1 in this question as well as the Canadian Pa-

cific Railway and we must always have aD interest in it.
We did that good service for the public. The public therefore has an interest in it. Now, the public ought to get the benefit of that service by paying the smallest possible rate in the way of freight or passenger charges. Suppose the company wishes to build 400 or 500 miles more road, and require this money. For what purpose do they require it? In the first place they require it in the interest of the public, as the public has demanded the accommodation, and that, I assume, should be fairly taken into consideration by the Governor in Council before they decide whether they will allow the company to sell more stock for the purpose of raising the money. They reach the conclusion that the money is needed in the interest of the public, and that it is proper to give that authority to the company. Then, I think they should consider, how can this service be supplied to the public at the smallest possible outlay? If the sale of $37,500,000 of stock will provide capital enough to supply what is needed, surely there is no justification for selling $50,000,000. Because if $50,000,000 of stock is sold, those who use these roads, either for the transportation of their goods or for travelling, must pay the interest on that $50,000,000. They could get lower rates if they only had to pay fixed charges on $37,500,000. It seems to me that this can be accomplished by putting the stock on the open market and selling it at the highest figures that it will bring. The Americans are doing this. They are compelling some of the companies that come and ask permission to sell stock, to sell it at public auction, realizing that the smallest amount of stock that can be sold for the most money is the best bargain that can be made in the interest of the public. If that is being done in the United States, I do not see why it could not be done in Canada. I have never yet been able to see either the wisdom or the justice of allowing men controlling a public utility, for which we pay large sums of money, to sell stock at 170 or even .150 and put $50 out of every $100 into their own pockets; using it, not to give a better service to the public, but only to increase their own wealth, and imposing upon the public the necessity of paying higher freight and passenger rates in the future.

I just wish to say that the company could raise all the money it requires to extend its lines if it would sell all its land in the Northwest at a reasonable price.
