This provides merely for the statutory increases and for six men of the outside service who have been brought into the inside..
The Government has been providing in the new Civil Service Act for increasing the salaries of the civil servants. Do they intend at the same time to keep up the old statutory increase?
I understand that the increases provided for in the Act will go on.
Does the minister mean the old statutory increase of $50 a year, to which every civil servant thought himself entitled, or the statutory increase provided for in the new law?
Under the old law, there is a provision for a statutory increase of $50. That is changed under the new law, and that $50 is included in this amount which we are asking now for next year.

Then will that statutory increase be continued or replaced by something else. Heretofore there was a very wide difference of opinion as to whether it was automatic or not. For a long time it was considered automatic, but ministers of this government have said that it was contingent on reports made by the deputy minister, and that even then each minister might exercise his judgment. The ex-Postmaster General (Sir Wm. Mulock) contended over and over again that he had no-right to give these increases and did not give them for several years.

As a general rule the increase will be given unless there be some record of want of diligence. In cases where there is such a record it will not be given. But as a rule it will be regularly given until the maximum is reached.

Is there any annual report on each official by the deputy head or only in cases where a report is asked for? If the statutory increase does not act automatically, there ought to be an annual report. If the increase is only given in such cases as the deputy head may recommend, injustice may be done to some official. There ought to be some fixed principle.

I understand from my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. FEBRUARY 2, 1909
Fisher), who is more familiar with the provisions of the new Act, that a report has to be made by the heads of the different branches every three months to the deputy head. The deputy head reports to the minister and his report also goes to the Civil Service Commission.
Does the Act provide for a statutory increase of $50 per year to all the Custom house officers in the outside service ?
It applies to none of them.

How are we to understand the operations of the Act of last year in conjunction with the Act which it is proposed to pass this session ? Here is an individual in the first division, subdivision A, whose salary last year was $2,700. Under the Civil Service Act, the minimum to which he would be entitled would be $2,800 in that division. I understand that $50 is the annual increase to which he will be entitled, beginning the first of September last. I would like to know whether, under the Act contemplated by the resolutions of the hon. Minister of Agriculture, this man will receive an additional sum of $150, making his salary this coming year $3,000, instead of $2,850.
Did my hon. friend cite the case of a clerk at $2,700?

His salary for 1908-9 was $2,700. It is proposed now to make it $2,850. I understand he is placed by the Civil Service Act of last session under subdivision A of the first division, of which the minimum salary is $2,800, and that his salary may go up, at an increase of $50 per year, until it reaches $4,000.	$50 has been
added to the $2,800, making his salary $2,850. My question is whether, under the Act foreshadowed by the resolutions of the Minister of Agriculture, this individual will have this year $150 in addition to the $2,850, making his salary $3,000 instead of $2,850. I understood the right hon. the leader of the government to say yesterday that such was the case.

I do not know the individual case, but this appears to be a man who was in subdivision B of the first division this present fiscal year, because he is getting $2,700, which is $100 below the maximum of that division. Apparently the department intends promoting him to subdivision A of the first division at $2,800. This item is wrong because in the first division the statutory increase is $100 and not $50. However, I am informed that this $50 is for the six months at the rate of $100 increase each year. Therefore, although this gentleman is to be promoted to subdivision A of
the first division and will get six months of the statutory increase of $100, he will practically get this fiscal year $2,850. He was in subdivision B of the first division on the first of September at $2,700. Under the resolution, to be eligible to get $150, he would be obliged to stay within his class, so that he would'only get $100. Therefore, under the resolution before the House his salary on the first of September will be raised to $2,800 and he will have that until his promotion takes place into subdivision A of the first division, when he will have $2,800, which is the minimum of that division, and then would get his statutory increase of $100 per year in the ordinary course.
The question I have asked is whether this particular individual will be entitled to the additional $150?

I said he would get $100
of the $150 on the first of September because he could not go above the maximum of his class until promoted. He would then be promoted and would get the ordinary statutory increase of $100 per year, which is to be provided for the coming fiscal year.

It does not seem to me that the Act is very clear, or else the explanation of the Minister of Customs and the Minister of Agriculture is wrong. My inquiry was whether the statutory increase was given automatically or whether it was contingent on something else. The answer was that it was contingent on a good report. To ascertain what is meant by that, let us turn to the Act. It is provided that the Civil Service shall be divided into two divisions, namely, the inside service and the outside service. The inside service is defined as consisting-
Of that part of the public service in or under the several departments of the executive government of Canada and of the Auditor General, the Clerk of the Privy Council, and the Governor General's secretary employed at the city of Ottawa, or at the Experimental Farm station or at the Dominion Astronomical observatory near Ottawa, but not including the officers, clerks and employees employed at Ottawa in the second or outside departmental division.
Now, when you turn to the Act to ascertain what record is to be kept of the employees, on which they are to qualify for increase, you find it provided that :
A record of the conduct and efficency of all officers, clerks and employees below the first division shall be kept in each department.
It appears by the first section that I have read that the first division is the inside service. And a record of all below this first division, or inside service, is to be kept. Surely that is not clear.

It seems to me quite clear. Under section 3, there is a clear definition

of what is meant by the inside service and what is meant by the outside service.
The inside service is the first division.
No, it is the inside service, and the inside service is divided into divisions and subdivisions.

The Act clearly says ' The Civil Service shall be divided into two divisions,' and the first of these divisions is the inside service. And section 40 provides for a record of conduct and efficiency of officers, clerks and employees below the first division.
That refers to divisions under section 5. If my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) will refer to that section, he will see that it defines the divisions and subdivisions.
If we are clear about that, let us understand this first case. As I understand it, this clerk comes under the Act in subdivision B and is getting a salary of $2,700.	"
Yes.
He goes into subdivision A, the minimum salary of which is $2,800. That is, he receives an increase of $100 by that promotion. Does that reduce the other increase by $100 ?

The general increase which we are now providing comes into force on September 1. At that date, this officer was in subdivision B at $2,700. Under the resolution which is now before the House, he gets as much off that $150 increase as his position in that subdivision permits- that is, he is not increased beyond the maximum of his sub-division.
So, he gets $100 ?

Yes, because $2,800 is the maximum of the division. Then, apparently, it is the intention of the Minister of Inland Revenue-about which I know nothing-to promote him into subdivision A of the first division, the minimum salary of which is $2,800. Therefore, he will receive that salary on going into the new subdivision.
He, at that moment, receiving $2,800 ?
Yes.

No, $2,800. He will be promoted into the other subdivision, the minimum salary of which is the maximum salary of the other. But he will be eligible for the statutory increase, wdiich, in the first division, is $100 a year. And apparently the accountant of the department has Mr. SPROULE.
provided for that occurring half way through the next. fiscal year, and has, therefore, only asked for $50 of the statutory increase instead of $100.
I suppose this holds with all these employees. Now, the regular employees under the old Act were 36 in number ?
Yes.
And the regular employees-so to call them for convenience sake -in this new schedule are still only 36.
They are given here at 42.
Six from outside.
Yes, six have been brought in. Now, I -would like to analyse that in the case of this department and see where we are. Who are these who are brought in from outside ?
They were paid out of outside votes.
What were the names, and what were they getting?

Lewis is one, he was getting $600; and doing clerical work. Can-tin was getting $500. Ekins was doing-clerical work, and getting $600. Then there were two messengers, Bourgouin, who is getting $750, and L. Roy, who is getting $500. Then there is provision made for Davidson, another messenger, at $500.
Provision made for a vacancy is not the addition of an outside man. Here you are taking in a number of outside men.
We are making provision for the appointment of another.
You have only transferred five men from the outside, now you want to add an extra man as messenger. How long had these five clerks been in the employ of the department?
Over a year.
All of them?
I would not be sure.

We would like to be sure. This is a test case of the working out of this
aggregation of laws.
Bourgouin has been on since June, 1903. I will get the rest of the information for the hon. gentleman during the evening.

I think there is an error in having it six, it should be five; then the one ought to be in the other column. In the next, the laboratory, you had eleven men, who seems all to have been brought in from the outside, and in the chief technical

engineer's branch the same. The same in the weights and measures, the same in the methylated spirits. I would like some information on all these. The minister may think this is calling for a good deal, but this is on a special occasion, and we would like to see how the thing is working out.
These are brought in under Act of Parliament.

But how will we know that all sorts of irregularities have not taken place in bringing them in? Now we are putting them where they go on the establishment, -where they have a regular status, where they can get all the advantages of the Civil Service Act. We want to know how they got in. We know that when they were in there last they came in through the door of examinations, and were regularly appropriated for. Here you are putting thirty-two new clerks on, and we want to know their status and standing before we translate them to this haven of rest.
Supposing you knew that, what good would it do? Under the law we are instructed to bring these men into the inside service, and we do that, even if they have only been on six months or three months.
The minister says he was compelled by law to bring in these six men. There were only five, and they wish to smuggle in another.

No provision was made for him last year. I will get the information the hon. gentleman asks for. But I will ask the hon. gentleman to note this. Take, for instance, the laboratory branch, where you have eleven men who have been paid out of outside votes. Parliament passed a law that these should be brought into the inside service, and we are simply carrying out the law and bringing them in. Now, does it matter whether these men have been in the outside service fifteen years, or one year, so far as carrying out the law is concerned? Must they not come in, and if so, what will be the value of these particulars the hon. gentleman is asking for?

What the law says in effect is that the men who have been in bona fide employ in the outside parts of the departments here, should be taken on at the salaries they have had. That may be done in many different ways. I am not saying this is not all proper and straightforward, but the question already put has brought out one fact, that you claim six men and you only had five.	[DOT]
We have a provision for that.
You are putting on a new man. In the same way, we would like to know with reference to these others.

Supposing I admit that this is a fact, that this one should have been put in the other column? No provision was made in the estimates of last year. Still I press my question on the hon. gentleman. I suppose that I could give the particulars with regard to each of these officers of the department. They have been bona fide in the service, but paid for out of the outside votes. Under the reorganization they will be bound to be brought in no matter whether their term of service has been for one, or five, or seven years. Therefore, I was asking the hon. gentleman whether any good purpose would be served by getting these particulars,-I do not object-as to how long each one of these had been in the service. Supposing he had been only a year, we would still have to bring him in under the law.
Suppose he had only been in one day?
Well, that would be running pretty close.
It would be running close, but it would be doing more than that; it would be showing a piece of sharp practice on the part of the minister.
It would depend on whether there was a necessity for the services of the officer when he came in.
Well, there is no need taking up an hour quarrelling over this. If the minister promises that we shall have the information let him give it to us pleasantly and we will get along all the better.
Is there any other information you want?
That is all I see at the present time.
Shall we pass this item?
Better get the information.
Shall we take the next item?

I imagine we will run up against the same thing with every other minister. I do not believe there is a minister prepared to give the information as to the hundreds and hundreds of men they are putting on the outside list. I propose to ask each minister, and I suppose that when I do each minister will reply that he does not know a blessed thing about it.
I do not think that is quite a fair statement of the case.
It may not apply to them all.

Personally I would be prepared to give the hon. gentleman that information. There are about 200 of my officers who have been paid out of the lump vote for the outside service but who have been working here in Ottawa and doing exactly the same kind of work as those in the inside service. By the Act of last session these people were all brought in. I confess that I did not have prepared a statement of all these officers and of their duties, but I will have it prepared.
You will find it in the Civil Service list.
No, I confess that they will not be found in the Civil Service list.
In my department they will be.
In mine they will not be. They were not in the inside service and they were not in the outside service according to the Act.
Of course, this is a thing which, when it is once done, is done.

I quite agree with that, but I do not think it is quite fair for my hon. friend to intimate that because we have not that information off hand we are trying to force the thing through. Knowing what the hon. gentleman wants I will have the information for him when the items are taken up. Perhaps it would be well to take up these items and discover what information is required and then we can leave them over until that information is obtained.
What shall we do meanwhile?
Go on with other government business that is ready.
We have this ready.
It does not seem so.
Is there any information wanted about the Inland Revenue vote?
Is there anything more than the general vote?
No.
This is for clerical assistance?
There is no change whatever. Suppose we go on to outside service of the Inland Revenue Department and see if anything is wanted there.
If the minister wishes it, although I suppose we will have the real man back here some day. Why not take the minister's own department-Customs?
There the same question will arise, I suppose.
Well, take the outside service.
The Deputy Minister of the Department of Inland Revenue has been granted leave of absence; I think he is going away on Thursday and I thought that perhaps you would allow his estimates to pass.

If you take up his estimates we will go through them.
Excise-salaries of officers and inspectors of excise, &c., to provide for increases depending upon the result of excise examinations, $426,400.05.

Would the minister
give us the particulars of that?
There is an increase of $9,277.49. This represents the regular statutory increases.
What will be the result if these officers do not pass the excise examinations?
They will not get promotion unless they pass.
Then, of course, the money will remain in the treasury?
Yes.
This $9,000 is simply for statutory increases for the present staff? Are there any additions?
No, I understand not.
This simply provides for the statutory increases which will come to the different officers after proper examination?
That is as I understand it.

I find on page 23 that $31,307.93 has been accounted for as for the services of men brought from the outside to the inside service. This increase of $9,277 would apparently be added to that making a total increase of $40,584.93.

No, that would not be connected with this. This is excise. There are none of the other items apparently in which there are any increases, so that there would not seem to be much room for explantation. It seems to be a very carefully prepared estimate : the vote has been kept down in every item except where it has been increased by statutory increase.
We would like to have this item divided into its various heads.

I could not do that off hand.
Item allowed to stand.
Stamps for imported and Canadian tobacco, $85,000.
Those are the stamps for placing on the tobacco. About that amount of money is required each year.
Where are those printed?
In Ottawa under contract.	*
What is this item of commissions?

As I understand the vote for the year before was $70,000 and this was spent within a few hundred dollars, and it is estimated that this year they will require this amount, but they cannot say how much will be left of the $85,000.
What is the commission?

This is the commission paid to collectors of customs for duty eol

lected by them, some $10,000; and a small item of $100 to the postmasters in Quebec who sell these twist tobacco stamps.
I was counting that commission in as part of the $85,000, but it is a vote by itself. Then I find all that was spent for the stamps was $69,577 in 1907-8.
Yes, that is right.
What has been sr>ent this year up to the present time?
We ought to be able to tell that but we cannot tell you how much was spent in the whole year.
But you can tell how much was spent until now on an estimate. It may be that the tobacco business has grown so that you require $15,000 more for stamps. That would be a pretty rapid growth.
Yes, it is growing. It can be got if the hon. gentleman insists upon it. I will try to have it after recess.

There is another point. You have a vote of $10,000 to pay collectors. In 1907-8 all you spent was $4,800. How is it that you want a little more than double that this year?

(Minister of Customs.) I presume my deputy is getting the information asked for before recess and is not here yet. Could we not pass the InInland Revenue items and give the information on other items?
It is hardly fair to ask the House to pass a million dollars or more just on good will. The minister should have made himself acquainted with his estimates, or should have had the deputy ready.
I am referring to the item under ' Civil Government.' That is not a million dollars.
The minister has not the information.
It will be here.
Then the minister wants us to pass the estimate and take the information afterwards?
All I ask is to close up this item 14, and then we will go on with Customs or Justice.
Well, if the minister has the information about these outside men we will go into that.
That was all that was asked for, and it will be here.
Then, let it stand until the information is ready.
But it keeps so many other items back. And what is the use?
The minister should have his work ready.
It was not anticipated that such questions would be asked.
Any deputy with a head on his shoulders, or any minister in charge of the estimates might have anticipated that such questions would be asked.
The deputy has a head on his shoulders, and so has the minister, and neither anticipated that-
Then it is time they did.
Before the item is finally passed, I would like to get some information with regard to this sum of $60,000 to enable the department to supply methylated spirits
We are proposing to let that stand in the meantime.
Item 94 stands. Eesuming item 14, Department of Inland Eevenue

The minister will see that we are up against the same difficulty as in item 294. The minister has not the information, and the deputy is not here. If the minister has any item ready, let us take that up, and wait until the deputy comes. Perhaps the Minister of Customs' own estimates are ready.

I explained the reason why I wanted to get this through. Of course, if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster), does not sympathize with it, all right. The deputy has been given leave of absence on account of impaired health, and this is the last night he can be here. I thought it would not be too much that the question asked might be allowed to remain, the information to be supplied by the department.
Is there nobody who can give the information?
No, no one ready.

No one is ready with such information as has been asked for, because nobody anticipated that such information was either necessary or desirable. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Aylesworth) is ready to go on with his estimates.
If the ministers are not ready, we cannot do business.
The ministers are ready to answer anything that will serve any good end.

Does not the minister see that we are doing here what has not been done before within my memory?-We are adding six or seven hundred names to the establishment. Does the minister expect us to pass such votes without asking ques-Mr. PATEESON.
tions? Why, it is simply absurd. I do not think there is another minister who would ask us to do that.

This is not a case of six or seven hundred names. In this item, we are adding five names, and these are simply taken in from the outside service. The hori. gentleman (Mr. Foster), asks the names. I do not object to that. But what purpose will such information serve? I ask the hon. gentleman that question. If any saving of money were proposed, or if there were any ground of legitimate criticism, it would be different. But such questions, as I say, were not anticipated. We say we wall get the information. Of course, if the hon. gentleman will not allow me to go on, I cannot go on.
Civil government-administration of justice -salaries, $94,648.75.
There is a large increase here.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. B. AYLESWOETH (Minister of Justice).
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The increase is merely apparent, not real; it is caused by the transfer of the salaries of a number of officials from different portions of the estimates to their present position. Under the amending Civil Service Act, the inspectors of penitentiaries, whose salaries were $3,100, are now called clerks in the first division, subdivision A., and their salaries are provided for in the third item on page 12 under the head ' Administration of Justice '-two clerks at $3,150. Before the statute of last session, that amount of $6,300 would have appeared under the head of ' Penitentiaries.' The increase is only the $50 statutory increase.
The names are Stewart and Dawson?	*

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, Mr. D. Stewart, and Mr. G. W. Dawson. In the same way, Mr. W. P. Archibald, the Dominion Parole Officer, was receiving a salary of $2,000. He was provided for previously under the head of the Penitentiaries Branch. He becomes a clerk in the first division, subdivision B. The effect is to-increase his salary by $100, $2,100 being the figure in that class. That is one case of an actual increase in the Department of Justice under the new classification. There are, I believe, seven such cases altogether in the department.
How much of a flat increase will he get?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I presume, though I speak without consideration, that he would be entitled to the full amount of the flat increase in addition to his salary. I ought not to make that answer without referring to the terms of the Civil Service Act. It depends whether or not he is at the maximum of his class. Then E. J. Adams, architect, penitentiaries branch, is another

official who was previously provided for under the head of penitentiaries. He now becomes a clerk in the second division of subdivision A, at the same salary as before.
What is his present salary?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: $1,650, there is no change. He was not classified until this year. He has now been classified in the second division, subdivision A, at the same salary as he had before. These four officers had salaries aggregating $9,850, and that is an apparent increase of that amount in the salaries of the Justice Department, whereas in truth it is merely a transfer in the estimates from one branch of the service to another. Then four clerks, by the operation of the recent statute, have become permanent clerks, whereas they were previously temporary, and provided for under the head of contingencies. These are T. Morris, $800 ; Miss L. M. Pillar, $550 ; a messenger Jobin, $700, and another messenger Hamel, $273.75. These are not cases of increase, but simply of transference from temporary employees to the permanent service.
What do they get when they come in ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The figures I have given. They are provided for in the items mentioned on page 12, under the head of Administration of Justice.
It reads there, $637.50 instead of $550.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am not sure whether the $637.50 item in the printed estimates is intended for Miss Pillar or not. If it is, as is possible, it is the annual increase which she would be entitled to before the end of twelve months, added to this $550.
Mr, FOSTER. The annual increase then would be $87.50. How do you make that out ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Assuming that the $637.50 is intended for Miss Pillar, it would be an increase of $87.50 over the $550 at which she stood on the 1st of September last ; and it is to be accounted for, I suspect, by the circumstance that she is intended to be recommended for a special increase under the statute, $50 in addition to the statutory increase, that is an annual increase on the whole of $100, and this $87.50 would be the fraction of that amount for the portion of the year after the anniversary of her entrance into the service would arrive. Then the two messengers stand at the same figures exactly as they were receiving previously.
$75 was added.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
One was $273.75
which, with the statutory increase, would
now be $323.75. One was $700, and $775 was intended to cover his salary. I do not know any reason for the $75 as distinguished from $50. I am not able at the moment to explain why that is $775.
One question with reference to the last four, when they were appointed to the service, or if they had been in the service for more than a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They were made permanent on the 1st of September last. When they entered the service I am not able to state without reference to papers that I have not with me. They were all in it when I took charge, and had been for some time. My statement that they were in it when I took charge is, I think, not applicable to the messenger Hamel. He is a boy, who was taken into the service by the deputy a year or more ago. He was there before the 1st of September, I cannot state when he came in. Then a further circumstance accounting for that apparent increase between last year's total vote and this year's, is in the increases which have been attendant upon the new reorganization scheme. Those increases aggregate $900, or $1,000 it will be, because one of the propositions which I had made when the brief from which I am speaking was prepared, has not been carried out.
These increases are, first, Mr. F. H. Gisborne, who, before the classification of last September, was receiving $2,450. He has been graded in the first division, subdivision
A,	at a salary of $2,800, which, with the statutory increase, would be the $2,875 item in the first division, subdivision* A, in the printed estimates. Mr. Gisborne is a barrister who has been a first-class clerk, or chief clerk under the old system in the department for many years. I do not remember exactly when he entered the service, but it was in the time of Sir John Thompson, eighteen or twenty years ago. Then, Mr. Chisholm, another gentleman of whom exactly the same thing can be said, a qualified barrister and discharging very important duties in the way of examining and certifying titles to properties which are bought for government purposes throughout the country, was recommended by .me to council for grading in the first division, subdivision A, but that recommendation has not been acted upon and he remains classified in accordance with the salary which he was receiving on the 1st September last; that was a salary of $2,000. He has been graded as in the first division, subdivision
B,	at a salary of $2,100; so that there will be an increase of $100 to him, an increase of $350 to Mr. Gisborne, $150 to Mr. Cote, who is the registrar of applications for clemency in the case of criminals, and who was receiving $1,950, but who goes into the first division, subdivision B, and so re-

ceives a salary of $2,100. Mr. Narraway, accountant of the department, received $1,900 before last September, he has been graded in subdivision B of the first division and now receives $2,100. He will thereby receive .an increase of $200. Miss Asselstine, stenographer, penitentiary branch, was receiving $800 before September; she is classified in subdivision A of the third division at $900, so that she will have an increase of $100. Mr. Archibald, parole officer, who was previously receiving $2,000 is now graded in subdivision B of the first division and will receive $2,100. These increases, by reason of the new classification, aggregate $1,000. Then, the difference between the figure of last year and that of this year is further accounted for by the statutory increases which I have detailed and which aggregate $1,225. Coming to the courts, which are now made branches of the department to the extent of being included in the classification under the new Civil Service Act, we have to some extent, the same thing occurring as in the department proper. There is an increase to Mr. L. W. Coutlee, the assistant reporter.
Will the minister take them in the order in which they are given here?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: This is the only increase by reason of the new classification. Following them in the order in which they are given here, the first item of $4,000 used to be statutory. It is now provided for in this vote. It provides for the registrar of the court. There is no change. The next two, in the first division of subdivision B, are the two reporters of the Supreme Court. There is an increase of $200 to Mr. Coutlee by reason of the reclassification. He had been receiving $1,900, he is now to receive $2,100, being graded in the first division of subdivision B. In the second division, subdivision A, are Mr. Lawson and Mr. Bligh, clerks in the Supreme Court, in whose case there is no change.
What is the salary of the other reporter?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Masters, senior reporter, was receiving $2,350 before September 1. There is no change. There are no other changes otherwise in the Supreme Court. In the case of all the other officials of the court they are graded in accordance with the salaries they were receiving on 1st September last.
They are the same as before?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The same individuals and the same salaries in each case. The same thing is true of the Exchequer Court. The salary of the registrar, which is $3,000, is not changed in'"amount, but it used to be Mr. AYLESWORTH.
provided for under the statute. Now it is included under Civil Government, otherwise there is no change. The same individuals are continued at the same salaries respectively being graded in accordance with the amounts they were previously receiving.
Do you also take the Dominion Police?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The Dominion Police, I should have mentioned, are in the same position as the two courts.
Who are these two officers?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The commissioner, Mr. Sherwood, provided for previously by statute, was receiving, I think, $2,950 previously and is now receiving $3,050 by a statutory increase of $100 from the 1st October. The other officer is Mr. Cawdron, whose salary was previously part of the Dominion Police appropriation and who is now to be provided for under Civil Government. He was getting $1,300 before and by the statutory increase from the 1st April he will be entitled to $1,350.
What are his duties?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
His duties are largely clerical as secretary and factotum of the commissioner, he and the commissioner constituting the staff except for the men on the force.
Contingencies, $10,400.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The explanation of [DOT]the decrease of $2,100 in this item is that the return which I had the honour to present to-day in regard to paroled prisoners was provided for in that $2,600.
You are not anticipating such another this time ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
No.

Did these go in at exactly the same salaries they were receiving?
They went in at the same. Of course, the statutory increase is always understood.
Why are there two additions?
The two extra assistant analysts were required and passed their examination before the Inland Revenue Board.
What extra work was put upon them?

The staff was short owing to the death of Mr. Macfarlane. Mr. McGill was promoted to Mr. Macfarlane's place, and the additional work necessitated these two appointments.
Chief electrical engineer's branch, $6,900.
There are six there. Does the hon. gentleman want the names and salaries of these?
Yes.

Higman at $2,800. The hon. gentleman knows that he has been a long time in the service. In July, 1901, J. A. Whyte, at $1,200; in June, 1906, C. J. Evans, at $950; in January, 1908, N. R. Cole, at $900; in May, 1908, E. D. K. Matthews, at $550; in January, 1908, M. E. E. McKell, at $500.
What were these men appointed to do? What is their particular work? ITow is it you have had to add so largely to the electrical branch?
Mr. Whyte is inspector of gas metres; Evans is a mechanical expert; McKell is a stenographer.

The information I wanted to get was this: You have added three to the electrical engineering branch during 1908, making six altogether. What is the extra work which has made it necessary to double the staff?
Three of them were temporary and were paid out of contingencies. There is no additional staff.
Although they were paid out of contingencies three of them were appointed in 1908. They were not working before that. How did you happen to double the staff in 1908?
Simply because of an increase of work.
That is not enough. Can you not find out what it was?
A general increase in the work of the department all the time. The deputy cannot specify.
This is electrical engineering work; what is the work they do?
Two of these mechanical experts adjust scales and metres. Formerly they were sent to outside places to do the work, but it is thought better to have it done in the department.
That disposes of two. What about the other one?
One is a stenographer.
The expense of examining and testing them before was paid out of contingencies, I suppose?
Yes, so I understand.
Does the department find that by employing the two the work is done at a cheaper rate or in a better way?

The work is better done.
Weights and Measures inspection branch, $5,000.

This covers the salaries of James Fyfe, first division, subdivision A, salary $2,800. E. C. Way, appointed in May, 1908, 3rd division, salary $800. Mrs. I-. Barbeau, 3rd division, appointed August, 1906, salary $500. T. Burgess, lower grade, appointed August, 1892, salary $900.
What necessitated the addition of Mr. Wade in May, 1908?

He is a thoroughly trained scale inspector, and the department thought they were fortunate in securing his services. Mrs. Barbeau is a typewriter and Mr. Burgess is a carpenter. In the methylated spirits, W. Armstrong, superintendent of warehouse, gets $2,000, appointed June, 1887. F. Parent, $1,200, appointed in May, 1891. James Hogan, warehouseman, appointed 1902, $900. F. H. Popham, assistant warehouseman, $750, appointed July, 1904.
Travelling expenses, rent, stationery &c., $90,000.
The items of this expense will be found in the excise report, page 136.
How much has been expended, so far, out of that amount ?

I cannot give the hon. gentleman that information.
Stamps for imported and Canadian tobacco, $85,000.

Up to November 30, the amount expended for tobacco stamps was $53,588.52, or at the rate of $82,482.80 for the present year. The demand for stamps cannot be calculated definitely, and sufficient stamps must be kept on hand to meet all possible demands of the trade. Of course, any unexpended part of the vote lapses at the end of the year.
The expenditure on stamps seems to be increasing rapidly.

Only through the increase of tobacco manufacture, I think.
To pay Collectors of Customs for duty collected by them, 1908-9, $10,000.
I see that in 1907-8 only $4,281 was expended. How is it that $10,000 is required ?
The years overlap the accounts do not come in, and some must be paid out of the next year. The amount given can hardly be taken as the yearly expenditure.
What amount has been expended so far this year ?
Nothing. The accounts will not come in until the end of the year.
If they come in at the end of the year, then this $4,281 must represent what was paid for 1907-8.
Yes, unless some came into the next year. They take amply sufficient in this vote to cover that.

That is it-the vote seems very large in proportion to the amount expended.
To enable the department to supply methylated spirits to manufacturers, the cost of which will be recouped by the manufacturers to whom it is supplied, and to pay for rent, light, power, freight, salaries, &c., $60,000.
Is this to supply the users of methylated spirits with cheap material ?
Yes.
What does it cost the government to make it, and at what rate is it supplied to manufacturers ?
It is sold at actual cost of manufacture-53 cents a gallon.
How many manufacturers use it ?
Hundreds of them-it is used very generally.

Have experiments been made with a view to furnishing agriculturists with a cheaper grade of methylated spirits or denatured alcohol ? I do not need to tell the minister of the opportunities afforded agriculturists in many of the countries of the world to procure cheap denatured alcohol for use as a source of power on the farm.
This is the cheapest the government has been able to produce, and, as the price is dearer than that of gasolene, gasolene meanwhile, keeps the lead.
But, if it can be made in Germany at 20 cents or 25 cents a gallon, is there any reason why we should not carry on experiments with a view to supplying it at a similar price ?

I am told that if you allow for the difference in the gallon measure of the two countries, it is not sold cheaper in the United States than here. In Germany, it is made out of potatoes, and the labour employed is paid wages that would not do for our people.
The only place of manufacture is Ottawa ?
Yes.
Does not the minister think it would be wise to manufacture in other places, for instance, in the Northwest ? The charges for freight from Ottawa to distant parts of the country must be enormous.
That is under consideration, I believe. There are no spirits, I think, manufactured in the Northwest, and the freight would be the same on that as on methylated.

One reason why the spirit is sold in Germany at a lower price than in Canada is that the German government pays a bounty on the production there, and that lessens "the price to the consumer in Germany.
Is this a new idea on the part of the government, to supply methylated spirits to the manufacturer at cost?
No, we have done it for a great many years.
How much was expended last year?
Can the minister tell us what is the customs duty on methylated spirits?
If it comes in under the head of spirits, $2.14 per gallon.
Have any experiments been made with it as a motive power to take the place of gasolene?
I am not aware that there have been any experiments made in this country, and the deputy doubts if there have been any made in the United States. Gasolene is cheaper.

I understand that experiments have been made in other countries, and that they have proved satisfactory. I am seeking this information on account of the manner in which gasolene has been utilized as a motive power in the west. We are rapidly working into gasolepe plough-15
mg, and things of that kind, and if we could get methylated spirits in free of duty it would be a great advantage to the agriculturists of the west. If the government would allow me to make a suggestion, I think it would be well for them to experiment along those lines and ascertain what its value would be as a motive power.

Power-ploughing i3 the coming system of ploughing, but power-ploughing when done by steam entails very heavy machinery. If you could do power-ploughing by gasolene or alcohol the machinery is much lighter, and you get over the whole difficulty of supplying a power plant with water and with fuel. The great trouble in power-ploughing now is to get water to the engine, and to get fuel to the engine. But if we could have gasolene or alcohol at a cheap rate there is no doubt the whole system of ploughing would be revolutionized, to the great advantage of the agriculturists. The suggestion made by my hon. friend (Mr. Staples) is well worth the attention of the government.
That is quite true, and if anything cheaper than gasolene could be found, it would be a great advantage. Methylated spirits at the present price cannot compete with gasolene.

If you, have not made the experiment it would be well worth a trial. There is a -large appropriation asked for here, some $60,000; I think it would be well to spend a portion of that in experimenting along those lines.

As I understand it, that this $60,000 all goes back again, that is the cost of producing methylated spirits that are sold to manufacturers for manufacturing purposes. The United. States government, for nearly ten years, have been taking a deep and active interest in the question of denatured alcohol for such purposes as the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Staples), and the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean) have mentioned. In the United States they can manufacture denatured alcohol cheaper than we can manufacture it in Canada from any of the sources from which we now do manufacture it. If we could manufacture it as they do in Germany, from potatoes, or in France, from sugar beets, we might perhaps produce it more cheaply than we do now from grain. But the United States can produce the ethyl alcohol from corn much cheaper than we can produce it from the grains we have in this country. They are experimenting in aid of agriculture, and have experts who for years have been carrying on special experiments along that line. It seems to me that it would be perhaps more prudent that our government should not spend any money for a year or two, but wait the re-



suits of experiments that are being carried on across the line.

I may say to my hon. friend (Mr. Miller) that if they have been experimenting with corn and such grain as they can grow to advantage in the United States, why can we not experiment with the grain we are growing in this country? I think it is not asking too much in the interest of agriculture to expend a portion of this large amount for that purpose. I would suggest that until we are able to produce methylated spirits in this country we should not exact such an enormous duty. Why not let this in from Germany, and let us have the benefit of it in the west until such time as you can put on the market a commodity that will answer the purpose for which we desire it.
There would be great danger in the matter of revenue, and there might be in other directions too, if you were to let it in free.

But the minister must see that cheap alcohol, outside of all questions of drink, is being used more and more in the industries, whether it be in the shape of methylated spirits, or used as a preservative, or in connection with science. I find an agitation all over the country, and you find it in the scientific press of other countries. _ The demand for cheap alcohol for industrial and other purposes is increasing, and it is well worthy the attention of the government whether we should not try and give the public cheaper alcohol than we do at the present time. I know there is a danger to the revenue, and that would have to be guarded against. But the American government have come to the conclusion that it is necessary for them, and that it is their duty to find a way of producing cheap alcohol for industrial uses.

Many requests come from my part of the country appealing to the minister to take off the duty on methylated spirits. I believe that if it were not for the enormous restrictions put on by this government it would be manufactured to a greater extent in the western country. The people there think it very strange that they should have to pay such an enormous price for this article that could be manufactured from the refuse of the products of the farm that are now practically going to waste. Potatoes, frozen and damaged grain and even straw could be utilized for this purpose. I think it would be well worth the serious consideration of the government to see if there could not be some means taken to permit of the manufacture of these products in the west. I hope the minister will think it over seriously.
The department are closely watching all the experiments that

are being tried in the United States. As far as I am aware none of them has been successful yet. In reference to the production of the Northwest, if there were a distillery there that was producing alcohol the department could easily permit the manufacture of methylated spirits, but I understand that alcohol is not produced in the west yet, and that until it is done I do not know how you could reduce the cost.
Weights and measures, gas and electric light inspection-salaries of officers, inspectors and assistant inspectors of weights and measures, $72,500.
There is an increase of $4,650.
That is due to new appointments and small increases of salary granted to deserving officials and in' no case exceeding $100.
What are the new appointments?
Bugeaud and A. B. Caldwell, appointed January 1, 1908, at $400 each.
Where are their districts?
Gaspe. H. Spicer and J. C. Thompson appointed at Winnipeg at salaries of $600 each. They are down for $100 more, so that they will be increased to $700.
Does the minister know the receipts of the Weights and Measures Department as compared with the expenses, and do the receipts come any where near paying the expenses?

The total revenue collected during 1908 was $83,021.32 as against $54,927.26 for the nine months ending March 31, 1907, and the total expenditure for 1908 was $101,492.24 as against $69,466.15 during the nine months ending March 31, 1907. So that it runs about that much of a deficit year by year.
Salaries of gas and electric light inspectors, $39,200.
The increase is due to-new appointments and small increases in salaries.
Who are some of the new appointees?

Mr. H. Fraser of Belleville, who was appointed on January 2, 1908; his present salary is $1,000. Mr. Ren-ahan of Toronto, appointed March 1, 1908, at a salary of $900; and Mr. Roche of Ottawa, who was a temporary employee, but has been made permanent.
How many inspectors of electric light meters are there?
About sixty altogether of gas and electric light.

The public are complaining about the inspection of electric meters. They have no knowledge that there are government officials who will inspect them, and it is complained that many companies through the country have their meters set to run fast.

The meters must all be inspected, I believe, on installation, and if any complaint is made subsequently it is attended to by an inspector. If the charge is not sustained, the person making the complaint pays for the inspection, and if it is well founded the company pays for the inspection.
A great many of these instruments are imported from the United States. Have the instruments to pass inspection by thp government before they pass customs?
No. They must be inspected before they are installed.

In towns?
Mr. fATERSON. Under the Inspection Act, any place.
If I owned a plant in a town of 5,000, imported my meters from Pittsburg and installed them in the houses myself, what protection is there for the public against these instruments?
You would be liable to a penalty.
Does that extend to villages?
Everywhere. For the year 1908, 41,062 were verified. Every five years I believe they are inspected.

I wish to support my hon. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. J. A. Currie) in the position he has taken in regard to this matter. In some of the smaller towns we experience trouble in getting the inspector to come and investigate the condition of the electric light plants and inspect the meters. In the town where I live we have trouble now and have had for some months, and the man who manages the plant in that town informs me that he has several times asked the inspector to come down from London and inspect the meters for him, but has been unable to get him to come.
Will the hon. gentleman give the name of the place so that the officer can be communicated with?
Petrolea, Ont.
That will be attended to by the deputy.

The question I asked has not been answered- how many electrical inspectors are . there besides the gas inspectors?
15i
The same men act in both capacities.
They must be good men, for it takes a high grade electrical engineer to inspect an electric meter.

It is a mechanical
test, I understand.
Who is the last inspector appointed?
Major Harris was appointed in January, 1908.
What was he doing before he was appointed?
I do not know.
Where did he come from?
Broekville, I understand.
Perhaps the Minister of Railways and Canals can tell us who this man was or what he was doing.

I do not know what he was doing immediately before his appointment, but he was a graduate of McGill University in electrical engineering and took very high honours. He had experience on the Pacific coast and was manager of the Broekville electric light for one year.
Metric system, to provide for the delivery of lectures and the publication of maps, charts, pamphlets, &c., $3,000.
What is being done in the way of lectures?
Nothing for the last two years.
Then why do you take the vote?
The money is expended in supplying metric sets to schools.
$3,000 worth?

No, it has not been
spent every year.
When are we going to have the system adopted?
I suppose that with the diffusion of these samples the people are being educated _ in the system, and when they are sufficiently educated to demand it I suppose it will come like other measures.
How much was spent last year?

What is the use of taking a vote for $3,000 when you only expect to spend $98? I thought this was a year in which the government were practising

economy. Does the minister think it is a good idea to take votes when you do not intend to spend the money?
We do not know what we may do.
If the minister does not know what he is going to do, on what basis does he ask parliament to give him the money?

The minister may perhaps expend more in the way of distributing the samples this year than he has done before.
Export of electric power, $2,500.
Will the minister tell us what this is used for? What organization has the government for the regulation of the export of electric power?
Under the law every company exporting electric power must apply for a license, and there is an inspection and travelling expenses connected with the work.
Is there an official in charge of it?
Yes, Mr. Higman has that under his charge.
Where can we find a report of what the official has been doing in the last year?

I am told there is a report; but I think a question on that subject was asked by the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) the other day and the answer will be found in Hansard.
Intercolonial Bureau of Weights and Measures, $216.
Explain that.

That is Canada's annual contribution to this bureau. This is not in reality an increase, but appears here owing to the fact that the supplementary estimates for the current year did not by an oversight include this amount.
Adulteration of food and fertilizers, under the administration of Act respecting fraudulent marking, $30,000.
How many convictions were obtained during the past year under this Act ?
Quite a number, but I have not the exact number.

The general impression is that the Act was not carried out very strictly, not only with regard to the adulteration of food but also of fertilizers. On looking at the report from the Inland Revenue Department, we find that there is a great deal of adulteration both of food Mr. FOSTER.
and fertilizers and it is important that it should be stopped.
My hon. friend is quite right. My deputy tells me that it is intended to bring in a Bill this session that will enable us to deal with the matter more efficiently than in the past.
Will it cover anything but fertilizers ?
No, only fertilizers.
Are fertilizers which come from the other side inspected ?
Yes.
How many officers are in the department for the purpose of enforcing the carrying out of the Adulteration of Foods Act ?
Sixteen confidential inspectors outside.
How much money was expended last year in salaries ?
$3,700 was paid.the inspectors and over $12,650 in the laboratory.
What is done when the samples of adulteration are collected ? Are the names published ?
The parties are prosecuted where fraud is intended and the names published.
Many a time the merchant might not be aware that the goods purchased are adulterated.
Yes, and it is then rather hard on him to publish his name.
When a manufacturer is found guilty of adulterating food products is a fine imposed ?
Yes, when he does it fraudulently.
Do the fines amount to anything serious ?
Not to a very large amount.

Would it not be advisable to increase very heavily the amount of fines in cases of fraud so that there would not be so heavy a drain on the finances of the department in connection with the Act. The general impression is that the fines are not heavy enough.
They are not very heavy, that is true.
Last year the amount of fines collected by the government on adulterated fertilizers was $10. Was that all the amount that was collected ?
I do not think there was over $150 collected altogether.

According to the papers there has been considerable adulteration of food product. Surely the minister will not admit that there has not been one instance in which a fine was imposed during 1908 for the adulteration of food.
There have been several but perhaps not as many as there should have been.

Where will we find it ? On page J-28 of the Auditor General's Report I find under the heading of fines and
forfeitures:

There is nothing there to show that there were any fines or forfeitures for adulteration of foods at all.

The country feels generally that it is highly important that the law against adulteration should be strictly enforced. It is only fair that the peopie who fraudulently adulterate food should pay a large portion of the cost of inspection.

I am informed that there have been a number of fines imposed. It appears in the Inland Revenue Report with other items-adulteration of food, fines
and penalties, $148.25-not a very large amount.

I find a list on page J-36 of the Auditor General's Report, under the head of 'Adulteration of Food,' and totalling $148.25. Does this mean that fines were collected from the men whose names were given?

In some cases the prosecutions may not have been pressed. Hon members can understand that, while the officers endeavour to enforce the law as best they can, yet an adulterated article may be found in the hands of an innocent holder, who would not know that he was violating a law.

Is not the remedy against the manufacturer? Is not his name on the package? And, if so, surely he can be held. I find that in Ottawa there are ten analysts and a dozen scattered over the country. This is a very expensive staff to keep up, and yet there seem to be no results to show what they have been doing for the enforcement of the law.

And I would like to know exactly how they find out what foods are adulterated. Here at page J-25 of the Auditor General's Report, is a list of salaries and contingencies under 'Food Inspection.' J. Hogan, Kingston, was given a
salary of $198.52; J. Talbot, London, $49.98; A E. Sanderson, Ottawa, $11.66; T. Kidd, Seaforth, $500; H. J. Dager, Toronto, $90.28; J. J. Costigan, Montreal, $350. Is there not a general inspector who goes to different places and collects samples?
The department send to their collectors of excise to procure samples of certain articles and forward them to the department. For this service, these officers are allowed a small sum.
What is the position of this man, T. Kidd, Seaforth, who was paid $500?
He devotes himself to that work and does nothing else. He is the only one.
His travel account amounts to $162.90. He cannot have travelled much for that.

I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. J. D. Reid) is right.
Miscellaneous-Proprietary or patent medicines, $5,000.

This will be required to meet the expense of administering the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act which comes into force April 1, 1909. A similar sum will be included in the supplementary estimates for the current year.

Has the minister any
details showing how it is intended to expend the money?
It will be necessary to pay expert medical men to ascertain what is necessary to constitute the proper medicines and so on. Also, literature will be necessary for distribution.
Have the officers been selected yet?

No officers are, being appointed. This is being administered by the present staff.
Department of Secretary of State-Salaries (including P. Pelletier at $3,000), $53,737.50; contingencies, $6,500.

In explanation of these estimates, 1 may say that the amounts are those at which all these officers were brought under the recent Civil Service Act with the exception of the Assistant Under Secretary of State. He has been senior chief clerk, and takes charge of the business of the department in the absence of the Under Secretary. He has had 21 years' experience in the department, and his duties include the supervision of certain applications under the Companies' Act, the applications that are made in the French language. The late Secretary of State, in view of Mr. Pelletier's duties, recommended that he should be

given this increase of $200. There are no new appointments in the department.
Are you positive?

Perhaps the hon. member refers to a position in the first division of subdivision B. That position is vacant by reason of the transfer of Mr. Foran, who was formerly in the department, and who has been made secretary of the Board of Civil Service Commissioners. That office is retained, but no appointment has been made to it as yet.
How many of those that were on as temporary officers were made permanent?
Three messengers, J. A. Jessop, J. Brankin and H. H. Duggan.
I think this item should have been allowed to stand over, because we did not expect it was coming up to-night.
The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) had some pertinent questions which he wished to ask the minister.
I shall be pleased to answer any questions to-morrow which any hon. gentleman may desire to ask me.
The minister said that Mr. Pelletier had an increase of $200. I see on page X-3 of the Auditor General's Report that he got $2,700 last year. Is that the same gentleman the minister refers to?
That is the same gentleman, he got an increase of $100. He came in at $2,800 at the minimum of that class. This provides for an addition of $200.
Are the gentlemen mentioned on page X-3 the same gentlemen who come in under this item of $30,000?
I think so.
When was H. H. Duggan appointed?
He was appointed last year, I think about seven or eight months ago, at a salary of $500.

I would like to get the
exact date to-morrow.
Is this a new item, $600 for a private secretary?
No, that is a continuation of the same item.
Formerly a private secretary was a first-class clerk. Is he now outside the Civil Service Act?
No.
Why is he listed here as in receipt of an allowance instead of listing him as an employee?
He would not get the $600 unless he were put in here in this way -allowance for private secretary. It is the same in all the departments.

Why is a change made in that particular method of doing it? In the Auditor General's Report the private secretary is included among first-class clerks. Is this an extra $600 given to an employee who gets another salary in another capacity?

No. I understand it has been the practice in the past to pay the $600 to a gentleman occupying a position in the department, whether he be a first class or a second class clerk. My information is that this amount has been paid for years past in the same way.
In the Auditor General's Report we see that A. Brophy gets $1,500 as a first-class clerk, then he receives $600 more for acting as private secretary.
That is correct.
Then my question was not properly answered. I asked whether .that $600 went to an employee who was already drawing a salary under another head, and the minister said no.
I did not so understand the hon. gentleman's question. If that is what he means, I must answer yes.
The $600 goes to an employee who is already receiving a salary in another capacity?
Yes.

Let us understand it. The private secretary of a department is taken from one of the clerkships. My own opinion is that the system is all wrong, but it has been the rule in this government for years My opinion is that a minister ought to be able to select his private secretary, pay him a straight salary, any salary he likes. The practice has been to take a private secretary from the employ of the department. He receives the salary that he gets as a clerk and this $600 is combined with it to make up his salary as a private secretary. This has been the practice for years. He does nothing as a clerk, he does his work as a private secretary, but he is taken out of the ranks of the clerks and given this salary.
Is this $600 extra allowance uniform in all the departments ?
Yes.
Plus whatever he received in the way of a salary as an ordinary employee ?
Yes.
Might I ask the minister to urge upon the government that they change this system and put into force the system that he has suggested to-night ?

Speaking for myself, I have always taken very strong ground, even before I came here, on this subject, believing that the minister should be in a position to select his private secretary from wherever he chose. But, it has been the custom to select him from the department and add this allowance to the salary that he is receiving as a clerk. There is now a clause in the Act which provides for a private secretary being taken in, but he must be brought in at the minimum of the class in which he happens to fall. Take my own private secretary as an example ; he was a temporary clerk and in order to get him as my private secretary I had to bring him in under the second division of class B at $800 and the $600 added only gives him a salary of $1,400, which is an absurd salary for the secretary in a department like that of Railways and Canals. He is brought in at the reorganization at $800 but in next year's estimates I am going to ask that his salary be placed on a fairly decent basis. The ministers are hampered in providing for their private secretaries by that rule, but it has been the practice in the past.

The practice originated in this way :	In former days a
minister would bring in a man who suited him and he would employ him as his private secretary. When the minister was going out of office he would ask for an appointment of some kind in the department in order that he might be retained. I imagine that is the way it arose.

Yes.

Give us an explanation of that.

The explanation with reference to Mr. Butler is that he being the deputy minister with a salary above that allowed by the statute, his name has to be mentioned. The name of Mr. Bell is also mentioned. He is the head of a branch that I have provided for in the estimates. He was brought into the department in 1900, I think. He is a very able man and his duties are to audit all the accounts in the department and in connection with all the railways throughout the country. If, for instance, a railway applies for a subsidy it has to prove that it has expended a certain amount and I have to send him all over Canada to audit these accounts. He has to meet the auditors of the Grand Trunk, the Canadian Pacific Railway and other companies. His salary is increased over $1,000. I want to bring him into the branch as the head of it. He is one of the ablest men in the service. In the reorganization under the Act I could only bring him in at the salary he was getting, but in the estimates for next year I name him so that there cannot be any question as to the legality of the matter. My private secretary is Mr. C. B. Robinson. I had to bring him in at $800 under the Act because he had to come in at the .minimum of the class in which he was employed being the second division of class B. I propose to give him a salary of $1,200 in addition to the $600 which will make his salary $1,800. There are two others whom I should mention. Mr. Bowden has been put in class A which will give him $300 of an increase and Mr. Alward who has charge of the law department and becomes the solicitor, the former solicitor having resigned some months ago, is put in class A, and his salary is raised several hundred dollars.
What position did he occupy last year ?	[DOT]
He was assistant to the law clerk.
Is he a barrister?
He is a barrister of standing and has been in the department for years. It is a very important branch and I am putting him at the head, of it as he is a very capable man.
How many men were brought in from the outside service ?
There are some in our department who have been working there since 1872, 1880 and 1890, but they were never made permanent. Some forty-five of these are now made permanent.
Were there any appointments in 1908 ?

Yes, Mr. McCrimmon, a young man, was appointed in the third di-

vision of subdivision B just at the beginning of 1908 at a salary of $650.
What is he doing ?
He is a clerk in the records branch.
Is he the only one ?
He was the only appointee in 1908. There were some in 1907.
How many in 1907?
Seven I think altogether. Of course these are appointed to vacancies that occurred; we made no new positions in 1907.
In 1908-9 the amount expended for this purpose was $63,000; but for this year it is $129,000, a difference of $45,000. Would the bringing in of the outside service make that difference?

There were some increases in the reorganization and some statutory increases amounting to a little over $8,000. My accountant informs me that we have several vacancies in our department that have existed for some time. We did not fill them last year, but we may fill them this year.
How are the vacancies caused?

In every department
there are so many clerkships. New ones are organized and old ones are sometimes dropped. These have been provided for for years in some cases and some men have been promoted, but during the last year we did not fill some of these vacancies. The reorganization of the department has taken place and one or two of these vacancies must be filled by the Civil Service Commission.
Does the commission make technical appointments too?
There is a clause that for special reasons appointments may be made upon the commission giving certificates.
If these vacancies have existed for a number of years, the minister must know that it is not necessary to fill them this year. What are the vacancies?

We found some of these in the outside and some in the inside service. In the reorganization of the service it ig almost impossible for the head of a department to see just how matters are going to work out under the new Act, and Mr. GRAHAM.
though we make provision for these vacancies, if we find that it is not necessary to fill any of them we will drop them. Under the old Act we could take a general vote and employ assistance under that, but under the new Civil Service Act we cannot do that, and in order to protect ourselves we make provision for these possible vacancies. Under this Act there is no elasticity. If we want a man in the department, we have to go to the commission and explain that there is a vacancy and we cannot promote unless a vacancy exists.
What is the total number of employees in the department?
Eighty-four. We are asking for 95, including these vacancies.
What will be the total increase of salaries under the new classification?
Under the classification coming into effect on September 1 the increase is $3,800.

Thirty-nine. The total number is now made up of both inside and outside employees.
